name: Imamates of Futa Jallon and Futa Toro
summary: Two Muslim Fula states created by religious revolutions: Futa Jallon in the Guinea highlands (1725–1896) and Futa Toro on the Senegal River (1776–1861). They ran Qur’anic schools and traded with the coast until the French took over.

knownFor.label: Rotating rule
knownFor.note: Two families took turns as Almami in Futa Jallon.

location.value: The Fouta Djallon highlands of modern Guinea; the article does not describe the Senegal River valley as its location.
location.source: Wikipedia: Imamate of Futa Jallon (checked 12 Nov 2026)

terrain.value: Futa Jallon is a high sandstone plateau with deep valleys, the source of the Gambia and Senegal (Bafing) rivers; Futa Toro lies on the Senegal River floodplain.

climate.value: Tropical savanna with a rainy season from about May to October; Futa Jallon is cooler and wetter, while Futa Toro is hot and dry, on the edge of the Sahel.

resources.value: Cattle and pasture, rice, millet and fonio, and in Futa Toro rich farmland flooded each year by the Senegal River; also hides for trade.

disasters.value: Droughts and locusts, especially in Futa Toro, brought famine; the Senegal River floods varied from year to year.

population.value: The article read gives no population estimate.
population.source: Wikipedia: Imamate of Futa Jallon (checked 12 Nov 2026)

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: Fula herders moved into the Futa Jallon highlands from about the 1500s; in the 1850s many people of Futa Toro left to follow Umar Tall east.

economicBase.value: Cattle herding and farming, much of it done by enslaved people in separate farming villages (runde), and trade in cattle, hides and captives.

tradeRoutes.value: Caravans carried cattle, hides, rice and captives from Futa Jallon to coastal rivers such as the Rio Nunez and Rio Pongo; Futa Toro traded with French posts on the Senegal.

wealth.value: The article says the Fula supplied grain and cattle to European neighbours (marked citation needed), and that the imamate sold enslaved people to European trading houses.
wealth.source: Wikipedia: Imamate of Futa Jallon (checked 12 Nov 2026)

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, market taxes and trade goods; cowrie shells in many markets.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

governmentType.value: An imamate; the first almamy was Ibrahim. From 1845 the Soriya and Alfaya factions alternated the post in two-year terms; a council of elders could remove the almamy (the article never says “elected”).
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Imamate of Futa Jallon (checked 12 Nov 2026)

keyRulers.value: Karamokho Alfa (Futa Jallon). Abdul Kader Kane (Futa Toro).

succession.value: In Futa Jallon the almamy was chosen in turn from the Alfaya and Soriya families; in Futa Toro the almamy was elected by a council of leading clerics.

institutions.value: In Futa Jallon a council of elders at Fugumba, the capital Timbo and nine provinces (diwe); Islamic law courts and Qur’anic schools in both states.

stability.value: Often unstable: Futa Jallon’s two ruling families fought over the post of almamy, and Futa Toro’s electors frequently removed almamys.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between the Alfaya and Soriya branches in Futa Jallon, and between powerful cleric families (the electors) and the almamys in Futa Toro.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry and foot soldiers drawn from free Muslim men, armed with spears, bows and imported muskets; fortified towns guarded against raids.

majorWars.value: Holy wars and raids against non-Muslim neighbours such as the Jalonke and the Solima of Falaba, and the Hubbu revolt against Futa Jallon from about the 1850s.

territoryChange.value: Little change in the core lands; Futa Jallon extended its influence over nearby peoples, while Futa Toro lost ground to the French on the Senegal.

alliancesRivals.value: Futa Toro fought and traded with the French on the Senegal River and with the Trarza Moors; Futa Jallon signed treaties with France from the 1880s.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; scholars produced Islamic writings and poetry in Pular using Arabic script.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to trade with the coast and to Muslim scholars, but hostile to non-Muslim neighbours and wary of European influence.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths across the highlands, canoes on the Senegal River, and messengers between Timbo and the provinces.

religion.value: Sunni Islam of the Maliki school, with Sufi brotherhoods such as the Qadiriyya and, later, the Tijaniyya.

languageWriting.value: Fula (Pular in Futa Jallon, Pulaar in Futa Toro), written in Arabic script (Ajami) for poems and religious texts; Arabic for law and scholarship.

artsArchitecture.value: Mosques with tall thatched roofs, such as those at Fugumba and Timbo, Islamic manuscripts, and religious poetry in Pular.

socialStructure.value: A free Fula Muslim elite of cleric and noble families above free farmers and craftsmen, with many enslaved people working the land.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to Islam, the almamy and one’s lineage; Fula identity and Islamic learning were sources of pride.

dailyLife.value: Farming and herding households in villages, with children attending Qur’anic school; enslaved people lived in separate farming hamlets.

neighbours.value: The Toucouleur Empire of Umar Tall to the east, French Senegal, the Trarza Moors, Mandinka and Susu peoples, and British Sierra Leone.

ideasReligions.value: An Islamic revival led by scholars who saw jihad and Islamic law as the basis of just rule; it inspired later movements such as Umar Tall’s.

riseSignals.value: Founded in 1725 by a Fulani jihad; Ibrahim won the Battle of Talansan in 1727.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Imamate of Futa Jallon (checked 12 Nov 2026)

peakPeriod.value: The early 1800s, when Futa Jallon’s schools and trade flourished and Futa Toro still controlled the middle Senegal River.

declineSignals.value: French expansion: Faidherbe’s forces took over Futa Toro (1859–61), and France occupied Futa Jallon after the Battle of Porédaka (1896).

outcome.value: Became part of French West Africa in 1896, after the French deposed Bokar Biro in November 1896.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Imamate of Futa Jallon (checked 12 Nov 2026)

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
